claims.text: Boride-based components naturally form loose Cr2O3/spinel oxide scales.
These naturally formed oxide scales provide insufficient protection against molten aluminum.
Hot-dip aluminization can form a uniform, thin Al2O3 film on boride-based components.
Controlling treatment temperature and immersion time ensures complete and uniform alumina-film formation.
The intervention produces a dense, continuous Al2O3 layer.
The Al2O3 layer adheres well to the boride substrate.
The alumina film is chemically inert toward molten aluminum.
The alumina film acts as a diffusion-resistant barrier that limits interaction between molten aluminum and the substrate.
The alumina barrier prevents penetration and reaction of corrosive species.
An alumina film is more protective than loose Cr2O3/spinel-rich oxide layers.
Hot-dip-aluminized components will exhibit less spalling and oxide disruption than untreated components after molten-aluminum exposure.
Hot-dip-aluminized components will have lower weight loss than untreated components after molten-aluminum exposure.
Hot-dip-aluminized components will retain greater structural integrity than untreated components after molten-aluminum exposure.
The protection will remain effective at typical hot-dip aluminum-plating operating temperatures.
Discontinuity or nonuniformity in the alumina film will compromise corrosion protection.
Operating above the alumina film's stability range will compromise corrosion protection.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement may vary with aluminization process parameters and film quality.

contradictions.description: The rule defines 'no statistically significant difference' using p < 0.05, whereas p < 0.05 conventionally indicates a statistically significant difference. A no-difference falsification criterion would normally require p >= 0.05 or, more decisively, an equivalence/noninferiority test with a predefined effect-size margin.
